content:
Your general approach is sound: given a good enough random bit generator (which is what your functions are), you can produce a good enough cipher by XORing plaintext with the bit stream. AES in OFB and CTR modes, for example, use the same trick.

The problem is that finding a sufficiently good and unpredictable PRNG is *hard*. You can't just write an arbitrary function (like `fx` in your code snippet) and expect it to work well -- that's going to be crackable. Instead, cryptographers settle on a single design and reuse it for all applications by changing the seed. AES is one example of such a design, and the seed is typically called a key.

In effect, what you've built is not a cipher but a cipher *framework*, and you've passed the responsibility of choosing the cipher onto the user. Which is kinda fine if that's what you're going for, but it's not a cipher per se. Real-world cryptographic libraries do use some of the methods you've applied, like chunking and MACs, but they don't typically expose them alone without the cipher itself.

content:
I applaud your desire to learn (and teach) cryptography. I'm a bit uneasy, however, with the idea that you're presenting your tool as something that someone might want to use. It emphatically *is not*, and you should make that *very clear*.

I am not a cryptographer, but I am aware that people who *are* cryptographers make mistakes that cause their systems to be completely ineffective. Are you confident you have not made any of these mistakes?

Allow me to provide an example: you suggest that a future improvement might "build a pool" of randomness. How will you protect that pool from attackers? Anyone who gets to peek at that pool will be able to decrypt everything you encrypt with it.

content:
I always understood the "without recompiling existing code, and while retaining static type safety" requirement as Expression Problem needing to be solved during compile time. The moment the solution is using dynamic dispatch during runtime, then it is no longer solution to "true" Expression Problem. But a weaker one, that no one argues is difficult.

The question that needs to be answered : When my solution is using Library A, that adds operations X, and Library B, that adds structures Y . When I compile my solution, will I get error that combination XY is missing? What would happen if A and B were loaded dynamically, and new version would add new operations or structures. When would the missing combinations be detected? Would I be forced to recompile with new version, thus being forced to use static loading of specific library versions?

content:
sig.params(x: Integer).returns(String)

It reads so wrong to me ...

Types in python aren't the prettiest thing either, but I found the syntax less distracting compared to Sorbet.

    Integer? instead of T.nilable(Integer)

So, compared to T.nilable it is better, but it is still not pretty.

    It can’t break compatibility with Ruby, or no one will use it.

I am not the main target audience, as I feel the whole slap-types-onto-ruby
is the wrong philosophy (thankfully matz isn't the biggest fan of it either), but this is not just about compatibility. It also is more code I have to maintain and I don't need any of the assumed "benefits". The type proponents claim that there are advantages in a large, shared code base; this may be the case, but of what benefit is it to me for solo projects? I don't have any of the problems the type afficionados claim are rampant in ruby (admittedly I use ruby quite differently to those people, who usually come from languages with mandatory and strict types, so their mindset is already very different to any "real" rubyist).

    There’s only so far you can go with “types as expressions,” but we could probably go a little further with optional monkey patches.

Please don't. Being able to duck-patch is nice for flexibility, but people get into a magic-rage and keep on writing the most complex, obfuscated code possible; and ruby makes this fun. Which is bad, because it often leads to utter gutter trash code. More magic, harder to maintain in many cases, and that includes about 80% of the DSLs out there.

> But I want to suggest one more option, which is a bit more radical: what if the Ruby VM parsed RBS comments and associated them with method definitions?

    class A
      #: (Integer) -> String
      def self.foo(x)
      end
    end

This is in comments? This could actually be useful, similar to how rdoc may be used. Having that as an option, if flexible, may be interesting; I could then use the first block as comment, including instructions how to use it; and the rest is additional information. (One could ask "but why not have it in code 1:1; I could focus on the code without having to think about the types, and at a later time work on the documentation, so I see this as having a bit more options available, just like when you write tests for code you could start either with the code, or with the tests.)

The one thing that is not solved is that all the type systems are quite ugly. There is probably no pretty type system (I am ok-ish with Haskell syntax, at the least compared to what else is available), but for some reason the python types annoy me significantly less than what has been proposed and implemented for ruby.
